paras: The lynching of George Witherell took place at Canon City, Colorado, early on December 4, 1888, when armed men broke into the jail, shot him and hanged him from a pole. Witherell had been returned to Canon City the day before to stand trial for the murder of a freighter, Charles McCain. The Associated Press account ran nationwide, dwelling on his fight in the cell and the other killings he was accused of.

According to a Pueblo dispatch of November 5, McCain had left Pueblo with two wagons and Witherell, who claimed to own a mine and hired him to haul ore. McCain's body was found buried at Turkey Creek, and Witherell was arrested in Denver with McCain's teams after Mrs. McCain doubted a letter signed with her husband's name.

Citizens of Canon City had then seized two trains they thought carried Witherell, intending to lynch him, but he was being held at Pueblo. Later reports said he had been pardoned about a year earlier from a life sentence for an 1872 killing, and was suspected in the disappearance of two men.

Taken to Denver after the first threats, Witherell was brought back on December 3 for a trial set for the end of the week. Sheriff Griffith tried to keep the return secret by leaving the train at Florence, but the news spread. By 11:30 that night several hundred armed citizens were in the streets, "determined to take Witherell from the jail and lynch him." The sheriff, whose family lived in the jail, held them off by pleading that he had a very sick child.

A little before 4 a.m. a voice at the kitchen door that connected with the jail claimed to bring a warning of an attack. When the sheriff opened it he was seized and gagged, while some twenty masked and armed men overpowered the guards and tore apart the steel cage that held Witherell. Witherell knocked several attackers down with a piece of his bedstead until three shots shattered his right arm and shoulder.

His arms were bound and he was marched to a telegraph pole near the penitentiary and hanged from the cross-bar. The Fort Worth Gazette said he was lowered after a few minutes, asked if he had anything to say, shook his head, and was hanged again. The body was left hanging until daylight, and the coroner cut it down late in the morning. Harry Perdue, another prisoner the crowd had threatened, was not harmed.

The coverage contains no report of an inquest verdict, arrests or prosecution of the lynchers. The Meeker Herald reported that "the verdict of the people at Canon" was that hanging was too good for him. The Delta Independent, by contrast, said the sheriff had been warned yet "made no determined resistance to the demands of the mob."

A Canon City dispatch of 11:30 p.m. on December 3 reported the siege the next day in Sacramento, St. Paul and Alexandria. The AP report of the lynching ran on December 5 from Seattle and Los Angeles to Savannah and Wichita, under headlines such as "GOT THEIR MAN," naming no race and calling him "the murderer" throughout. Weeklies ran shorter versions over the next ten days, calling him a "four-times" or "quadruple" murderer.

The Fort Worth Gazette headlined its special "A VILLAIN'S FATE" and likened his hanging to "the pulling up of a hog." The Rock Island Argus, in partial contrast, headed its report "a Relapse into Barbarism That Is Very Common" while still calling him "the notorious murderer." In Colorado, the Meeker Herald presented the hanging as just deserts, and the Delta Independent paired criticism of the sheriff with contempt for a "cowardly desperado."

The AP and the Fort Worth Gazette put about twenty men in the jail; the Rock Island Argus said one hundred. The Argus also said the body hung until every resident had seen it, and the Delta Independent placed the hanging on a lamp post, not a telegraph pole. One digest said he severely wounded three men, where fuller dispatches say he knocked several down, and the killings attributed to him ranged from three to four, though only McCain's had been charged.

bases: A group of armed men broke into the Canon City jail, took Witherell, an accused murderer awaiting trial, and hanged him from a pole (A6, A10, A24).

Witherell was shot and hanged by about twenty (or one hundred) armed men who overpowered the sheriff and took him from jail, acting on the murder charges against him before his trial (A6, A9, A10, A11).

The AP report (A6), a separate Fort Worth special (A9, A10), a separate Canon City dispatch in the Rock Island Argus (A11) and two Colorado weeklies (A24, A27) agree that Witherell was taken from the jail and hanged early on Dec. 4.

accounts.label: AP wire report
accounts.gist: Twenty armed men entered the jail at 4 a.m., overpowered the sheriff and tore down the steel cage; Witherell fought with part of his bed, was shot in the shoulder, and was hanged from a telegraph pole and left until daylight.

accounts.label: Fort Worth Gazette special
accounts.gist: A hundred-man crowd was refused in the evening; before 4 a.m. a ruse at the kitchen door let about twenty masked men seize and gag the sheriff; Witherell, shot, was hanged twice near the penitentiary and cut down by the coroner late in the morning.

accounts.label: Rock Island Argus dispatch
accounts.gist: One hundred heavily armed men did it; a rope was slipped over his head in the jail, he refused to pray, and the body hung until every resident had viewed it.

accounts.label: Colorado weeklies
accounts.gist: The Meeker Herald said the sheriff was bound and gagged and Canon's verdict was that hanging was too good for him; the Delta Independent said he was hung to a lamp post and that the sheriff made no determined resistance.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'GOT THEIR MAN', 'A VILLAIN'S FATE' and 'Met Min Just Deserta' called Witherell a 'murderer' throughout and presented the lynching as deserved.
The Rock Island Argus headlined 'Pent-up Anger Finds Vent' with the deck 'a Relapse into Barbarism That Is Very Common', while its text called him 'the notorious murderer'.
Most papers ran the AP paragraph or a one-line digest item.
The Delta Independent faulted the sheriff for weak resistance yet called Witherell the most 'cowardly desperado' that ever lived.

conflicts.note: The several hundred citizens (A3) and the hundred-man mob (A10) were the evening crowd; both the AP and Fort Worth accounts put about twenty in the break-in.

info: About 4 a.m., Tuesday, December 4, 1888, after a crowd gathered at the jail the evening of December 3
Taken from the jail at Canon City (also printed 'Canyon City'), hanged a short distance away from a telegraph pole near the penitentiary (one item says a lamp post)
George Witherell (also Witherill, Witherel, Wetherell, Witherall; initials given as George R., George B. and J.), about forty years old

Charged with the murder of Charles R. (or K., or C. W.) McCain/McKain near Canon City in late October 1888; also accused or suspected of killing two other men (and, by some accounts, of an 1872 killing for which he had served a prison term)
Armed, masked men of Canon City, called 'citizens' and a 'mob'; not named
Harry Perdue (Perda, Perdu), another prisoner threatened by the crowd, was not molested
